meta.description: Genuinely Buddhist — but the English is Paul Carus's 1911 hymn "Self-Reliance," a verse rendering of Dhammapada 165, not a literal translation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'No one saves us but ourselves. No one can and no one may. We ourselves must walk the path'?
meta.ogDescription: Traced to Paul Carus, Buddhist Hymns (Open Court, 1911), p. 19 — a versified Dhammapada 165. The popular form drops his rhyming fourth line.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: c. 563 or 480 BCE – c. 483 or 400 BCE · Founder of Buddhism
answer.sourceLine: The exact English appears as the hymn “Self-Reliance,” headed “Dhammapada, 165,” on p. 19 of Paul Carus’s Buddhist Hymns (Chicago: Open Court, 1911) — the scanned book is online ↗. The teaching is canonical, but Carus’s quatrain is a free versification: Max Müller’s translation of verse 165 says only that “no one can purify another.”
answer.confidenceText: Verified to a dated, published source — though these exact English words are Paul Carus’s 1911 verse rendering of Dhammapada 165, not a literal translation of the Pali.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Buddhist Hymns: Versified Translations from the Dhammapada and Various Other Sources, Adapted to Modern Music
Versified by Paul Carus (1852–1919). Chicago: The Open Court Publishing Company, 1911
Dhammapada 165 (Chapter XII, “Self”), with the closing line tracking Dhammapada 276

source.excerpt:
By ourselves is evil done,
By ourselves we pain endure,
By ourselves we cease from wrong,
By ourselves become we pure.

No one saves us but ourselves,
No one can, and no one may;
We ourselves must walk the path,
Buddhas merely teach the way.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ lists the full quatrain in its Dhammapada section — not among the misattributed entries — citing verse 165 and Paul Carus, and adding that a circulating variant of the fourth line has never been located in Carus’s original publications. Quote Investigator ↗ has no article on the line.

Wikiquote points to Carus’s pamphlet The Dharma (1896), but the Internet Archive’s full text of the 1896 third edition ↗ contains neither “no one saves us” nor “walk the path” anywhere in its 70 scanned pages.

The wording is in a different Carus book: Buddhist Hymns (Chicago: Open Court, 1911) ↗, where p. 19 carries a hymn titled “Self-Reliance,” headed “Dhammapada, 165,” set to music by Carus. Its second quatrain is the quote, word for word. His foreword describes the book as his own versifications of “these ancient and venerable stanzas.”

The Pali behind it is narrower. Max Müller renders verse 165 “By oneself the evil is done, by oneself one suffers… Purity and impurity belong to oneself, no one can purify another,” and verse 276 “You yourself must make an effort. The Tathagatas (Buddhas) are only preachers” (Wikisource ↗). Carus fused and heightened the two into a singable rhyme.
source.excerptNote: The popular three-sentence version is the second quatrain only, with the rhyming last line dropped and the commas and semicolon turned into full stops.

artifact.linkText: Buddhist Hymns (Open Court, 1911) at the Internet Archive

source.rightsNote: The Pali Dhammapada is ancient and long out of copyright, and the English wording here comes from Paul Carus’s Buddhist Hymns, published in the United States by The Open Court Publishing Company in 1911 — well before the 1931 threshold, so it is in the public domain in the US. Note that this applies to Carus’s 1911 verse specifically: modern Dhammapada translations are separate works and remain under their own copyrights or licences.

author.name: Gautama Buddha
author.heading: The Buddha, and the verse behind the hymn
author.metaLine: c. 5th–4th century BCE · Indian ascetic and teacher; founder of Buddhism
author.bio: Siddhārtha Gautama was an ascetic and teacher in ancient northern India whose followers became the Buddhist community; Wikipedia gives his dates as c. 563 or 480 BCE to c. 483 or 400 BCE and notes that scholars still disagree by more than a century. He wrote nothing: his sayings were preserved orally and later fixed in the Pali canon, of which the Dhammapada — a collection of 423 verses — is the most quoted book in the West. Every English “Buddha quote” is therefore a translator’s sentence as much as his, which is exactly what makes this one worth tracing.

misattribution.heading: What gets muddled
misattribution.intro: This one is real — a rarity among “Buddha quotes.” But almost every version circulating online misstates where it comes from, and three things in particular get muddled.

items.who: Presented as a literal translation of the Pali
items.why: Carus was writing singable hymns, not a crib. Müller’s translation of Dhammapada 165 ends “Purity and impurity belong to oneself, no one can purify another” — there is no “saves” and no “path” in it. Carus’s closing line tracks verse 276 instead: “You yourself must make an effort. The Tathagatas (Buddhas) are only preachers” (Wikisource ↗).

items.who: The Dharma, or The Religion of Enlightenment (1896)
items.why: Wikiquote attaches the quatrain to this Carus pamphlet, citing “Ch. 165, as translated in The Dharma, or The Religion of Enlightenment; An Exposition of Buddhism (1896) by Paul Carus” (Wikiquote ↗). Searching the Internet Archive’s full text of the 1896 third edition ↗ and the 1898 printing ↗ turns up no occurrence of “no one saves us” or “walk the path.” The lines are in Buddhist Hymns (1911).

Wikiquote notes this variant has circulated for some years but “is not yet located in any of the original publications of Carus” (Wikiquote ↗). The 1911 hymn reads “Buddhas merely teach the way” — and the popular three-sentence version drops the line altogether, taking the rhyme with it.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Buddhist in substance and genuinely traceable in wording — to Paul Carus’s hymn “Self-Reliance,” printed under the heading “Dhammapada, 165” on p. 19 of Buddhist Hymns (Open Court, 1911) ↗.

context.heading: Why a Buddhist verse rhymes in English
lead: Paul Carus (1852–1919) was a German-American philosopher and the first managing editor of the Open Court Publishing Company in Chicago. Per Wikipedia ↗, his interest in Buddhism deepened after the World’s Parliament of Religions in 1893; The Gospel of Buddha followed in 1894, and he later sponsored D. T. Suzuki’s translation work.

Buddhist Hymns went a step further than translation. Carus’s foreword explains that he had “frequently been induced to try my hand at the versification of these ancient and venerable stanzas,” and he set several of them to Western tunes — German chorals, folk melodies, and settings of his own — so that a congregation could sing the Dhammapada. That hymnal impulse is why this line scans, rhymes, and travels so well: it was built to be sung, not to be literal.
context.detailsSummary: What Carus wrote in prose, before he wrote it in verse
detailsBody: In The Gospel of Buddha (1894), Carus had already rendered the same two verses in plain prose, in his chapter on the Dhammapada: “By oneself evil is done; by oneself one suffers; by oneself evil is left undone; by oneself one is purified. Purity and impurity belong to oneself, no one can purify another. You yourself must make an effort. The Tathāgatas are only preachers.” The full text is at Project Gutenberg ↗.

Set the two side by side and you can watch the famous line being made. “No one can purify another” becomes “No one saves us but ourselves”; “the Tathāgatas are only preachers” becomes “Buddhas merely teach the way.” Nothing is falsified — but the memorable words are the hymn-writer’s, not the translator’s and not the Pali’s.
context.pull: We ourselves must walk the path, Buddhas merely teach the way.
